claim: Homer's Iliad, Book 3 (lines 121–180) shows Helen 'on the walls of Troy watching the Greek heroes below, pointing them out to the Trojan king Priam — a scene known as the viewing from the walls.'
issue: Lines 121–180 of Iliad Book 3 is Iris's visit to Helen in her chamber and her leading Helen to the walls — not the teichoscopia (viewing from the walls) itself. The scene where Helen actually names Greek heroes to Priam (the teichoscopia proper) begins at line 181 and runs to line 244. If a student describes lines 121–180 as showing Helen pointing out heroes to Priam, they are wrong: at line 180 she has not yet named anyone. The full teichoscopia passage is lines 121–244. The lesson's description of what these lines contain is factually incorrect regardless of whether OCR prescribes 121–180 or 121–244 as the extract.
correct_fact: Iliad Book 3: lines 121–180 = Iris visits Helen in her chamber and leads her to the Scaean Gate walls. Lines 181–244 = the teichoscopia proper, where Helen identifies Agamemnon, Odysseus, Ajax and Idomeneus to Priam. The prescribed passage for the 'viewing from the walls' should be cited as lines 121–244 (or at minimum the description of what occurs in 121–180 must be corrected to 'Iris visits Helen and brings her to the walls,' not 'Helen pointing out heroes to Priam').

claim: The lesson defines 'anakalypteria' as 'the veil worn by an Athenian bride, which the groom lifted at the wedding ceremony.' The in-text parenthetical says 'her anakalypteria (veil)' when describing what the bride dedicated to Artemis. The glossary entry defines anakalypteria as 'The veil worn by an Athenian bride; the lifting of the veil by the groom was a central ritual act.'
issue: Anakalypteria does not mean 'the veil.' It means 'the unveiling' — the ceremony or ritual act of removing the veil, or the gifts exchanged at that moment. The veil itself was called the kalyptra (or kredemnon). The bride dedicated her kalyptra to Artemis, not her anakalypteria. Defining anakalypteria as the physical veil is a category error that could cause students to misuse the term in the exam.
correct_fact: Anakalypteria = the unveiling ceremony/ritual (literally 'the act of unveiling'), or the gifts given at the unveiling. The bridal veil itself is the kalyptra (or kredemnon). The bride dedicated her kalyptra (veil) to Artemis before the wedding. Anakalypteria refers to the ceremonial act of the groom lifting the veil, not the veil itself.

claim: Hesiod's Works and Days, 'lines 54–105, is the prescribed literary source for Pandora.'
issue: The standard scholarly citation for the Pandora passage in Works and Days begins at line 53, not 54. The Diotima resource (a widely used Classics scholarly database) explicitly titles it 'Works and Days 53–105.' The passage begins with Zeus's response to Prometheus's theft of fire at line 53. Multiple academic sources use 53 as the opening line. If the OCR prescribed booklet uses 54, this is fine, but if it uses 53, students citing 54 may lose the opening verse of the prescribed passage.
correct_fact: The Pandora passage in Hesiod's Works and Days is most commonly cited in scholarship as lines 53–105. Line 53 opens with Zeus's anger at Prometheus, which is the starting context for creating Pandora. The lesson should give '53–105' or verify the exact OCR booklet line numbering before specifying 54.

claim: Livia 'was eventually deified (made a goddess) under the emperor Claudius in AD 41.'
issue: The year of Livia's deification is stated as AD 41. Claudius became emperor in January AD 41, but Livia was deified by him in AD 42, not 41. Britannica and World History Encyclopedia both give AD 42 for the deification. A student citing AD 41 would give a factually wrong date.
correct_fact: Livia was deified by Claudius in AD 42, not AD 41.

claim: The Hegeso Stele glossary definition reads: 'A marble grave relief from Athens, attributed to the sculptor Callimachus, commemorating a woman named Hegeso' (repeated in the content_html dfn tag).
issue: No authoritative source attributes the Hegeso Stele to the sculptor Callimachus. Smarthistory, Britannica, and World History Encyclopedia all describe the sculptor as unknown/anonymous. The Callimachus known from ancient sources was associated with the lamp at the Erechtheum and possibly the Corinthian capital — no major reference connects him to this stele. This is a fabricated attribution that would directly mislead students answering source-description questions.
correct_fact: The sculptor of the Hegeso Stele is unknown. The stele is not attributed to any named sculptor in any authoritative source.

claim: 'For three days each autumn, citizen women left their households' at the Thesmophoria (in Athens).
issue: The passage specifically describes the Athenian Thesmophoria. Britannica confirms that while the festival lasted three days in most of the Greek world, in Attica (the region containing Athens) it was extended to five days. Describing it as three days for Athens is inaccurate and would be imprecise in an exam answer about this specifically Athenian festival.
correct_fact: The Thesmophoria in Athens (Attica) lasted five days, not three. Three days was the duration in other parts of the Greek world.

claim: The Bassae Frieze depicts 'Greeks fight Centaurs (the Centauromachy)' on one set of slabs, alongside the Amazonomachy.
issue: The battle depicted on the Bassae Frieze is specifically the Lapiths fighting the Centaurs — the Lapith Centauromachy at the wedding of Peirithoos — not 'Greeks versus Centaurs' generically. The British Museum, Britannica, and World History Encyclopedia all identify the combatants as Lapiths, not Greeks. Students learning this as 'Greeks vs Centaurs' would give an inaccurate identification and miss the specific mythological narrative.
correct_fact: The Bassae Frieze Centauromachy depicts Lapiths (a specific tribe, not 'Greeks' generically) fighting Centaurs at the wedding feast of Peirithoos. The subject should be named as 'Lapiths and Centaurs' or 'Lapith Centauromachy'.

claim: The lesson opens: 'On a late summer day in AD 79, the citizens of Pompeii and Herculaneum were going about their ordinary business...'
issue: Describes the AD 79 eruption as occurring on 'a late summer day.' Modern multidisciplinary evidence (a charcoal graffito dated XVI K Nov = 17 October; coin hoard minted September AD 79; botanical remains of autumnal fruits; heavy clothing on victims; volcanic ash wind-direction modelling from a 2022 study) now places the eruption on 24–25 October AD 79. This is mainstream scholarly consensus and OCR examiners are aware of the debate. Teaching material that asserts 'late summer' without caveat would mislead students preparing source-evaluation answers.
correct_fact: The eruption is now most commonly dated to late October AD 79, with 24–25 October the most widely accepted date based on multidisciplinary evidence. The traditional August 24 date derives from a disputed reading of Pliny's manuscripts. The lesson should either give October 79 or note that the date is debated.

claim: Collapsible section on Pompeii, Herculaneum and Ostia states the towns 'were buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79' without dating issue, but the same lesson's context frames the eruption as 'late summer' (implicit through shared narrative with lesson 5).
issue: The opening of Lesson 5 (same unit) sets 'late summer' as the narrative, and Lesson 1 references the eruption date uncritically. Independently, the Key Fact box in Lesson 1 states 'Over 80 thermopolia have been identified in Pompeii alone.' Most scholarly sources give approximately 80 thermopolia identified; no mainstream source supports a count definitively over 80 — the figure is more accurately given as 'around 80' or 'approximately 80'. Claiming 'over 80' overstates the evidence slightly.
correct_fact: The number of thermopolia identified at Pompeii is typically cited as approximately 80 (some sources give up to 89 as an upper estimate). The phrase 'around 80' or 'approximately 80' is more accurate than 'over 80.'

claim: The lesson refers to Petronius's Satyricon: 'the famous "Dinner with Trimalchio" episode (Satyricon 29–50)'.
issue: The chapter reference 29–50 is wrong. The Cena Trimalchionis (Dinner of Trimalchio) occupies chapters 26–78 of the Satyricon, not 29–50. Chapter 26 is where the invitation and preparations begin; the episode continues to chapter 78. Giving the wrong chapter range is a fabricated citation detail that would lose marks in a source-attribution question and undermine student confidence in the material.
correct_fact: The Cena Trimalchionis occupies Satyricon chapters 26–78 (some sources number slightly differently but all place the start no later than chapter 26–28, and the end at chapter 78). The lesson should cite it as 'Satyricon 26–78' or simply 'the Cena Trimalchionis section of the Satyricon.'

claim: The Temple of Apollo is described as standing 'just to the west of the forum, its columned porch facing onto an open precinct.'
issue: The Temple of Apollo is correctly placed on the west side, but it does not strictly stand 'just to the west of the forum' as a separate structure at a distance — it is integrated into the forum precinct on its western boundary, sharing the forum's western flank. More importantly, the lesson says its columned porch faces 'onto an open precinct.' Sources confirm the sanctuary has a portico of 48 Doric columns surrounding the central temple, not a simple 'columned porch.' Describing it as a 'columned porch facing onto an open precinct' understates the scale and could confuse students comparing it with the Temple of Jupiter.
correct_fact: The Temple of Apollo at Pompeii is surrounded by a colonnaded precinct (portico) of 48 Doric columns, with the temple on a podium in the centre. The sanctuary is bounded on the west side of the forum area. The description 'columned porch' should be 'colonnade-enclosed precinct' or 'portico with 48 Doric columns.'

claim: The bronze Apollo statue at Pompeii is described as 'showing the god in a striding pose, his arm raised as if drawing a bow.'
issue: The original bronze Apollo is an archer figure — his arm extended with a bow. 'Arm raised as if drawing a bow' is a reasonable paraphrase of the archer pose, but the Getty Exhibition and other authoritative sources describe the statue specifically as 'Apollo as archer' (Apollo Saettante) with arm outstretched to shoot, not 'raised.' The description is not factually wrong but 'arm raised' is imprecise — the arm is extended forward/outward, not raised above the head.
correct_fact: The bronze Apollo is in the archer (Apollo Saettante) pose: arm extended to shoot. The phrasing 'his arm raised as if drawing a bow' is ambiguous and slightly misleading; 'arm extended as if shooting a bow' is more accurate.

claim: Pliny the Younger, writing to a friend, describes the sounds of a bath complex next to his house — the grunting of weightlifters, the splashing of plunges and the calls of vendors selling snacks (Pliny, Letters 1.9).
issue: Misattribution of a famous ancient source. The passage describing bath noise — weightlifters grunting, vendors shouting, bathers plunging — is from Seneca, Epistulae Morales 56 (written to Lucilius). Pliny Letters 1.9 (to Minicius Fundanus) is about how city life fragments one's time with trivial obligations; it contains no description of baths or their sounds. Students citing 'Pliny 1.9' for this evidence in an exam would be citing a non-existent source.
correct_fact: The source for the noisy bath-complex description is Seneca, Epistulae Morales 56. Pliny Letters 1.9 is about the difficulty of spending time meaningfully in the city and has nothing to do with baths.

claim: Horace's Satires (2.2) mentions the Saturnalia as a time of relaxed rules and indulgence.
issue: Wrong poem number. Horace Satires 2.2 (Ofellus poem) is about plain, frugal eating and has no Saturnalia content. The Saturnalia in Horace is found in Satires 2.7, in which the slave Davus uses the Saturnalian licence to speak freely and criticise his master. Students who look up 2.2 will find nothing about the Saturnalia and will be unable to use this citation in an exam.
correct_fact: Horace's Saturnalia reference is in Satires 2.7, where the slave Davus exercises the freedom allowed to slaves during the Saturnalia to lecture his master Horace.

claim: The exterior is divided into four levels, the lower three decorated with arches framed by engaged columns in the three architectural orders: Doric on the ground floor, Ionic on the second and Corinthian on the third.
issue: The ground-floor order of the Colosseum is Tuscan (a Roman simplification of Doric with an unfluted shaft and plain capital), not Greek Doric. Multiple authoritative sources — Smarthistory, Britannica — note this distinction explicitly. While some sources use 'Doric' informally, at GCSE Classical Civilisation level where architectural orders are a named topic, calling it 'Doric' rather than 'Tuscan' is a meaningful inaccuracy. Additionally, the fourth level is described only as 'a solid attic storey with small windows', omitting that it has Corinthian pilasters and the corbels that supported the velarium mast poles — features that are architecturally significant.
correct_fact: The ground floor of the Colosseum uses the Tuscan order (Roman variant of Doric). The three lower orders are Tuscan, Ionic, Corinthian. The fourth (attic) level has Corinthian pilasters and corbels for the velarium awning masts, not simply small windows in a plain wall.

claim: The Mycenaean Warrior Vase is described as 'a large painted storage jar from Mycenae' found in 'the House of the Warrior at Mycenae'.
issue: The object is a krater (a mixing bowl used for diluting wine with water), not a storage jar. The correct building name is 'House of the Warrior Krater', not 'House of the Warrior'. Calling it a storage jar misidentifies the vessel type, which is a basic testable fact for OCR source analysis questions.
correct_fact: The Warrior Vase is a krater (mixing bowl), c.1200–1100 BC, found by Schliemann in the House of the Warrior Krater immediately south of Grave Circle A at Mycenae, now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

claim: Miltiades had 'first-hand experience of Persian methods of fighting, having served a Persian-controlled Chersonese on the Black Sea coast before returning to Athens'.
issue: The Thracian Chersonese (modern Gallipoli Peninsula) is on the Hellespont / Dardanelles, not the Black Sea. These are different bodies of water roughly 200 km apart. A student who repeats 'Black Sea' in an exam would be giving incorrect geographical information.
correct_fact: The Thracian Chersonese is the peninsula bordering the Hellespont (Dardanelles) on the European side — modern Gallipoli. It has no Black Sea coastline.

claim: The Key Fact panel states: 'The Greeks held the pass for two full days against repeated Persian assaults.' The conclusion also says the 'three-day stand allowed Athens to regroup its fleet', creating a direct internal contradiction.
issue: The battle lasted three days in total: two days of conventional fighting in the pass, followed by a third day comprising the last stand after Ephialtes' betrayal was discovered. The Key Fact panel — the highest-salience revision element — states only two days, which is the figure students will memorise and write in exams. Herodotus, Britannica, World History Encyclopedia and all mainstream sources consistently give three days.
correct_fact: The Battle of Thermopylae lasted three days: two days of fighting in the pass, then a third day of the final rearguard action. The Key Fact panel should read 'three days' not 'two full days'.

claim: Athens sent a runner, Pheidippides, to ask Sparta for military aid. The Spartans said they would help but could not march until 'the full moon festival was over'.
issue: The Spartans' reason for delay was the Carneia, a sacred nine-day festival of Apollo during which warfare was forbidden. Describing it only as 'the full moon festival' is imprecise — the Carneia was tied to a lunar date but had a specific name and religious identity that OCR students are expected to know. The flashcard answer ('a religious festival') is acceptably vague, but the main body should name the Carneia.
correct_fact: The Spartans could not march because of the Carneia, a sacred festival of Apollo. Spartan law forbade fielding an army until the festival concluded. Pheidippides arrived during the Carneia and was told to wait.

claim: A centurion was identified by distinctive equipment including 'armour worn on the left rather than the right (the reverse of ordinary soldiers).'
issue: The distinguishing feature was the SWORD (gladius) position, not armour position. Centurions wore their gladius on the LEFT hip, while ordinary legionaries wore theirs on the RIGHT. There is no evidence that armour was worn differently left-vs-right as a rank marker. The lesson has confused sword-side with armour-side. This misattribution would directly mislead students answering source-analysis or describe questions about centurion identification.
correct_fact: Centurions were distinguished from ordinary legionaries by three emblematic items: a transverse crest (crista transversa) on the helmet, a vine stick (vitis) of office, and — as a sword-side distinction — the gladius worn on the LEFT hip (ordinary legionaries wore theirs on the RIGHT). Armour positioning was not a left/right rank marker.

claim: The Roman marching-camp ditch was 'V-shaped, typically around 1.5 metres deep and 1.5 metres wide.'
issue: Vegetius (De Re Militari) gives the standard minimum ditch as 5 Roman feet wide × 3 Roman feet deep (approximately 1.52 m × 0.91 m). The lesson's stated depth of 1.5 m is roughly double the Vegetian standard. While larger ditches existed for more permanent positions, the quoted figure significantly overstates the depth for a typical marching camp and could cost marks if a student reproduces it as authoritative.
correct_fact: The standard Roman marching-camp ditch (fossa) was V-shaped, approximately 5 Roman feet (c. 1.5 m) wide and 3 Roman feet (c. 0.9 m) deep according to Vegetius, though dimensions varied with the size and permanence of the encampment.
